title: Thomas More
hookLine: the king's good servant, but God's first, executed for refusing the oath

lines: A GOLD CHAIN AND A FUR COAT.
THE KING ASKS FOR AN OATH.
cards: There's a portrait of him, painted in his lifetime. A dark coat trimmed with fur. A heavy gold chain across his shoulders, the mark of a man in the king's service.
A face that looks clever and a little tired. Lawyer, writer of a book called Utopia, friend of the king, and for a time Lord Chancellor of England.

Under the fine coat, tradition says, he wore a rough shirt of hair against his skin, to keep himself humble. Then the king broke with Rome, and asked for an oath. And the man in the gold chain went quiet.

teach.b: More stepped down as chancellor as Henry pulled the church in England away from Rome.

teach.h: HE REFUSES THE OATH, AND STAYS SILENT.
teach.b: Then came the oath. Leading men were asked to swear to Henry's new marriage and the order behind it.
More, as the usual account goes, was willing to accept who would inherit the crown, but would not swear to words that set aside the pope's authority over the church.

He refused, and refused to say why, hoping silence would protect him, since he had said nothing against the king. He was sent to the Tower of London. His daughter Margaret visited him there and begged him to give way.
He didn't. He was tried, convicted on testimony he said was false, and beheaded.

teach.h: THE KING'S GOOD SERVANT, BUT GOD'S FIRST.
teach.b: Tradition reports that on the scaffold he said he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Notice the order. He doesn't call himself the king's enemy.
He calls himself the king's servant, and a good one. He just won't put the king first.

Peter and the apostles, ordered by the council in Jerusalem to stop preaching, said it in the King James Bible: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Catholics honor More as a saint and a martyr of conscience.
There is more to remember. As chancellor, More pursued Protestants hard. He wrote fierce books against William Tyndale, and some of the people he hunted as heretics were burned.
The story holds both: brave and hard, a conscience that would not bend for a king, and a chancellor who pressed hard on the consciences of others.

how: Catholics honor Thomas More as a saint and martyr, keeping his feast together with John Fisher's, and he is honored as a patron of statesmen and politicians; Anglicans and others also remember him for his conscience.

games.q: you're Thomas More, in the Tower. your daughter begs you to swear the oath and come home. what do you do?
o: refuse, and keep silent about why.
games.why: he refuses, and stays silent. he is tried anyway, and tradition reports he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

practice: Name, quietly, the things that ask for your loyalty: work, family, friends, a team, a country, a cause, a faith, and let them line up without ranking them.
Then ask which one you'd keep if two ever pulled against each other, and hear the answer without arguing. If you pray, bring that question to God; if you don't, let it settle.
